answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and the wording is exact. It appears in Welch’s 2001 memoir Jack: Straight from the Gut, written with John A. Byrne, in ch. 24, “What This CEO Thing Is All About” — directly beneath the section heading “People First, Strategy Second.” A full-text search inside the scanned book ↗ returns the heading and the sentence together, in four separate scanned editions.

People First, Strategy Second
Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more important than developing a strategy.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence under Jack: Straight from the Gut (2001) and cites it to Ch. 24 — the only sourced attribution among the quote sites carrying this line.

Searching the scanned text directly settles it: Open Library’s search-inside index ↗ returns “People First, Strategy Second / Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more…” inside four separate scanned editions of the Welch memoir.

The chapter checks out independently: a study guide to the book ↗ gives Ch. 24 as “What This CEO Thing Is All About” and summarises its argument as getting the right people mattering more than strategy development.

And the framing is corroborated outside the book: strategy+business’s review of the memoir ↗ reports “People first, strategy second” as Welch’s mantra, alongside his remark that he would kill GE’s strategic planning process.
source.excerptNote: The heading and the sentence are reproduced here as they are returned by full-text search across four scanned editions of the book. The paragraph continues past the point the search snippet cuts off, so what is shown is the opening of the section rather than the whole of it.

author.bio: John Francis “Jack” Welch Jr. ran General Electric for two decades, from 1981 until his retirement in 2001, and became the most imitated — and most argued-about — American chief executive of his generation. He was famous for dismantling GE’s elaborate corporate planning apparatus and replacing it with relentless attention to who held which job, a preference he later condensed into the line on this page. His memoir Jack: Straight from the Gut, written with John A. Byrne and published the year he stepped down, is where that preference is stated most plainly.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right — unusually so for a quote this widely shared. What goes wrong is everything around the name: the source vanishes, the wording softens, and the thought gets folded into a different author’s book published the same year.

items.scope: Circulated with no source at all
items.why: Most listings give the sentence and a name and nothing else — Quotlr’s Welch page ↗, for instance, prints it as “Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more important than developing a strategy. — Jack Welch” with no book, chapter or year. That is how a genuine quotation ends up looking indistinguishable from a fabricated one.

Collins’s Good to Great argues that great leaders “first got the right people on the bus (and the wrong people off the bus) and then figured out where to drive it” — a separate formulation, in a separate book, that Collins’s own site ↗ presents without any reference to Welch. The two lines make the same argument and are routinely swapped for each other; neither one is the other’s source.

items.who: Later business books and course notes
items.why: Searching the same phrase across scanned books turns up loosened forms alongside the real one — “put people first and strategy second (getting the right people in the right jobs is crucial…)” among them, per the Open Library full-text index ↗. Variants like “Get the right people in the right jobs — it is more important than developing a strategy” are compressions of Welch, not quotations of him.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Welch’s own, word for word, and it has an address: Jack: Straight from the Gut (2001), ch. 24, under the heading “People First, Strategy Second” — as Wikiquote ↗ records and a search inside the scanned book ↗ confirms.

context.heading: Why he put it that way
lead: Welch spent his career at war with the corporate planning function. The strategy+business review of the memoir records him saying, long before he ran the place, that if he ever became CEO he would “kill this strategic planning process” at GE — and once he got the job he largely did, replacing thick planning books with argument, and treating the annual talent review as the meeting that actually decided the company’s direction.

So the sentence is not a throwaway aphorism about hiring. It is Welch summarising his own operating theory at the end of a 500-page account of running General Electric: that a company’s plan is downstream of its personnel, and that time spent perfecting the former at the expense of the latter is time wasted. He wrote it in 2001, the year he handed the company over — which is why chapter 24 reads less like narrative and more like a list of things he wanted to leave behind.
context.detailsSummary: Where it sits in the book
detailsBody: Chapter 24, “What This CEO Thing Is All About,” is where the memoir stops narrating and starts summing up — the last of the book’s substantive chapters, with only two short ones (ch. 25, “A Short Reflection on Golf,” and ch. 26, “New Guy”) and an epilogue after it. Rather than continuing the story, it distils Welch’s conclusions into a run of short headed sections — and “People First, Strategy Second” is one of them. The quoted sentence is the first line under that heading.

That structure is why the line travels so well: it was written to be quotable and to stand alone, which is unusual. Most quotations that circulate this cleanly turn out to have been compressed by someone else along the way. This one was compressed by the author.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more important than developing a strategy." under the heading Jack: Straight from the Gut (2001) and cites it to Ch. 24. The page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.

Full-text search inside scanned books returns, in four scanned editions of Jack Welch's Jack: Straight from the Gut, the text "People First, Strategy Second Getting the right people in the right jobs is a lot more"; the same search also returns paraphrased forms in other books, e.g. "put people first and strategy second (getting the right people in the right jobs is crucial".

Full-text search for the phrase "right people in the right jobs is a lot more important" returns hits inside Jack: Straight from the Gut by Jack Welch (multiple editions) plus later business books quoting it.
The Internet Archive record for Jack: Straight from the Gut gives the authors as Jack Welch (1935-) and John A. Byrne, publisher Warner Books, New York, publication year 2001, 524 pages.
Chapter 24 of Jack: Straight from the Gut is titled "What This CEO Thing Is All About" and argues that getting the right people is more important than strategy development.

The strategy+business review of the memoir states that "People first, strategy second" was Welch's mantra, and records his remark that if he ever became CEO he would kill GE's strategic planning process.

Jack Welch was born 19 November 1935 and died 1 March 2020; he was Chairman and CEO of General Electric from 1981 to 2001; his 2001 memoir Jack: Straight from the Gut was co-written with John A. Byrne and published by Warner Business Books, New York.
Quotlr's Jack Welch page prints the quotation with no source, book, chapter or date - only the attribution "- Jack Welch".

Jim Collins's site describes the Good to Great concept "First Who, Then What" - leaders who "first got the right people on the bus (and the wrong people off the bus) and then figured out where to drive it" - and does not mention Jack Welch.
